screens.title: The steam above your baking
lines: See that white wisp curling above your fresh-baked muffins? That's water pulling its favorite trick: shape-shifting.
Liquid to vapor to cloud to rain — water changes costume constantly, but it NEVER disappears. Earth has been recycling the same water for about 4 billion years.

vocab.meaning: liquid water gaining energy and escaping into the air as invisible vapor (a gas)
water vapor cooling back into tiny liquid droplets — clouds are exactly this
water falling from clouds as rain, snow, sleet, or hail
water gathering in oceans, lakes, rivers, and underground, ready to cycle again

sequences.title: The Expedition Shelf: Side Quests for the Curious

screens.title: Side quests for the curious
lines: Welcome to the Expedition Shelf — side quests for the curious. Collect them all!
Moon secrets, drifting continents, dancing particles, and the tiny rooms life is built from: every discovery here unlocks a weird-fact card.

vocab.meaning: the shape of the Moon's sunlit part as seen from Earth
the imaginary pole Earth spins around once a day — tilted about 23.5 degrees
a giant slab of Earth's outer shell that drifts a few centimeters per year
the smallest building block of every living thing

items.prompt: Follow one drop of water from the oven steam all the way around the planet and back.

steps.text: Oven heat gives water molecules in the cake enough energy to fly off as vapor — that's EVAPORATION. True vapor is an invisible gas; the white wisp you see is already the next step happening.
When vapor meets cooler air, it slows down and clumps into tiny liquid droplets — CONDENSATION. That wisp of 'steam', a fogged mirror, and every cloud in the sky are all the same trick.

check.question: So what is a cloud actually made of?
options: Billions of tiny liquid water droplets
Invisible water vapor
Smoke from faraway kitchens

steps.text: Inside a cloud, droplets bump and merge until they're too heavy to float — then they fall as PRECIPITATION: rain, snow, sleet, or hail, depending on the temperature.

Fallen water gathers in oceans, lakes, and rivers, and soaks underground — COLLECTION — until the Sun lifts it again. Earth has run this loop for about 4 billion years, so your next sip may once have been dinosaur spit.

check.question: Why doesn't Earth run out of water?
options: Clouds manufacture brand-new water
The same water keeps cycling around — nothing is lost
Volcanoes brew fresh water every day

items.prompt: The Case of the Shrinking Water Bowl: Amal fills her cat's bowl, and three sunny days later it's nearly empty — but nobody saw the cat drink. Finish the detective's note.

lines: Day by day, sunlight warmed the bowl until liquid water escaped into the air as invisible vapor.

items.hint: It's the process that lifts water UP and out — the cycle's first move.
items.explanation: Evaporation turned the liquid into vapor, molecule by molecule. The water didn't vanish — it just changed costume and joined the air.

items.prompt: Now you run the weather tower. Finish the storm report from Rainshadow Isle.

lines: Vapor rising off the sea cools into cloud droplets: [[condensation]]
The droplets grow heavy and fall as rain: [[precipitation]]
Rainwater drains into rivers and the lake below: [[collection]]

items.hint: Cloud-forming, then falling, then gathering — in that order.
items.explanation: Condensation builds the cloud, precipitation drops the water, and collection gathers it for the next round trip. The cycle never clocks out!

items.prompt: After Amal washes the baking sheets, the puddles on the counter vanish by morning. Which process turned that liquid water into invisible vapor?
options: Evaporation
Condensation
Precipitation
Collection
items.hint: The water went UP and out, as a gas.
items.explanation: Evaporation is liquid water gaining enough energy to float off as vapor. The puddle didn't vanish — it joined the air.

items.prompt: Label the four stages of the water cycle on the diagram.
items.hint: Up as vapor, cloud up high, fall back down, gather below.
items.explanation: Evaporation lifts water up, condensation builds the cloud, precipitation brings it down, and collection gathers it to start again. Melting and freezing aren't pictured here.

items.prompt: Amal's cat claims the window seat on a cold morning, where the glass is fogged with tiny droplets. Which process fogged the glass?
options: Condensation
Evaporation
Precipitation
Transpiration
items.hint: Warm indoor air touched cold glass — did water go gas-to-liquid, or liquid-to-gas?
items.explanation: Water vapor in the warm room air cooled against the cold glass and condensed into droplets. It's the same trick that builds clouds!

items.prompt: Complete the explorer's definition.

lines: A watershed is all the [[land|ground]] that drains its rainwater into one river or lake.

items.hint: Not the water itself — the stuff the rain falls ON.
items.explanation: A watershed is an area of land: every drop that falls inside it eventually drains to the same river or lake. You're standing in one right now!

items.prompt: Where is MOST of Earth's water found?
options: In the salty oceans
Frozen in glaciers and ice sheets
In rivers and lakes
Underground in aquifers
items.hint: Spin a globe — which color takes over?
items.explanation: About 97% of Earth's water is salty ocean water. All the freshwater together is just a few drops out of every hundred.

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about Earth's water supply — tap the lie.

truths: About 97 out of every 100 liters of Earth's water are salty ocean water
Most of Earth's FRESHWATER is frozen solid in glaciers and ice sheets
data.lie: Most of Earth's freshwater flows conveniently in rivers and lakes

items.hint: Think about where the fresh 3% actually hides.
items.explanation: Rivers and lakes hold under 1% of the freshwater — most of it is locked away as ice. The thin liquid slice we can actually reach is precious.

items.prompt: Ride along with one raindrop! Put its round trip in order, starting at the sunny sea.

sequence: The Sun warms the sea, and the drop evaporates into invisible vapor
Rising high, the vapor cools and condenses onto a speck of dust in a cloud
The droplet merges with others until it's heavy enough to fall as rain
On a hillside, the drop trickles downhill into a stream
The stream returns it to the sea, ready for the next lap

items.hint: Up as gas, cloud up, fall down, flow downhill, home to the sea.
items.explanation: Evaporation → condensation → precipitation → collection. The same drop has been making this trip for billions of years.

items.prompt: Mystery: Amal's icy lemonade glass is 'sweating' droplets on a hot day, but the glass doesn't leak. Finish the detective's notes.

lines: Summer air secretly carries lots of invisible water [[vapor|vapour]].
Touching the cold glass, that vapor cools and turns back into liquid — a process called [[condensation]].

items.hint: The droplets came from the AIR, not from inside the glass.
items.explanation: Air always carries invisible vapor; chill it and it condenses. The glass 'sweat' is the sky's cloud trick in miniature.

items.prompt: The potions classroom at wizard school runs its own tiny water cycle above the cauldrons. Label the diagram — and beware the two trick labels.
items.hint: Two of these processes are real but not pictured: one happens in plant leaves, one flows over land.
items.explanation: Transpiration (plants breathing out vapor) and runoff (water flowing over land) are real water-cycle extras, but the four core stages are evaporate, condense, fall, collect.

items.prompt: Match each water word to its meaning.

pairs: Evaporation
liquid water escaping into the air as vapor
Condensation
vapor cooling back into liquid droplets
Precipitation
rain, snow, sleet, or hail falling from clouds
Transpiration
plants releasing water vapor through their leaves
Aquifer
an underground layer of rock and gravel that stores water

items.hint: Two are sneaky newcomers: one involves leaves, one involves underground rock.
items.explanation: Transpiration is the plants' secret entrance to the water cycle — one big oak can breathe out hundreds of liters a day. Aquifers are nature's underground water tanks.

items.prompt: Water-saving showdown: which typically uses MORE water — a 10-minute shower, or running one full dishwasher load?
items.answer: The shower — about 80 liters, several times what a dishwasher load uses
options: The shower — about 80 liters, several times what a dishwasher load uses
The dishwasher — big machines use far more than showerheads
They use almost exactly the same amount
It's impossible to compare water use between them
items.hint: A showerhead pours about 8 liters every MINUTE. Multiply!
items.explanation: Ten minutes at roughly 8 L per minute is about 80 liters, while a full modern dishwasher load uses around 15. Shorter showers are one of the easiest water-saving moves there is.

items.prompt: A cloud-studies goblin wrote this weather report. Tap the sentence with the error.

segments: The Sun heats the lagoon, and liquid water evaporates into invisible vapor.
The vapor rises and cools high above the island.
A cloud forms — a floating puff of water vapor, which is why you can see it.
Inside the cloud, droplets grow heavy and fall as precipitation.

items.hint: One sentence forgets that true water vapor is invisible.
items.explanation: Clouds aren't vapor — they're billions of tiny liquid droplets (or ice crystals) made by condensation. If you can see it, it isn't vapor anymore!

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about water's superpowers — find the lie.

truths: The water in your glass has been recycling for billions of years — a dinosaur may have sipped it first
Water dissolves more substances than any other liquid, earning the nickname 'universal solvent'
data.lie: Clouds manufacture brand-new water that has never existed on Earth before

items.hint: Earth's water supply is a closed loop.
items.explanation: Clouds only carry recycled vapor lifted by evaporation — Earth has been reusing the same water since before the dinosaurs. No new water is being brewed up there.

items.prompt: Rain falls on the ridge behind a wizard school: drops on the east slope drain to the River Wyrm, drops on the west slope drain to Lake Lumen. The ridge is the boundary between two…
options: Watersheds
Aquifers
Deltas
Estuaries
items.hint: Each side of the ridge sends ALL of its land's rain to a different home.
items.explanation: Each slope is its own watershed — all the land draining to one river or lake. The ridge line between them is called a divide.

items.prompt: Legendary: Amal's showerhead pours 9 liters per minute, and she trims her daily shower from 10 minutes to 6 (about two K-pop songs). How many liters does she save in a 7-day week?
items.hint: Find the liters saved per shower first, then scale up to the week.
items.explanation: She saves 4 minutes × 9 L = 36 liters a day, and 36 × 7 = 252 liters a week. That's about a bathtub and a half of water!

items.prompt: Legendary: a desert town pumps water from its aquifer faster than rain can soak down to refill it. If nothing changes, what happens over the years?
items.answer: The water table drops, and wells must be drilled deeper and deeper
options: The water table drops, and wells must be drilled deeper and deeper
Nothing — underground water can never run low
The aquifer instantly refills after every rainstorm
Ocean water seeps across the desert to replace it
items.hint: An aquifer works like a bank account: pumping is a withdrawal, rain soaking in is a deposit.
items.explanation: Aquifers refill slowly — sometimes over centuries — so heavy pumping lowers the water table and can dry up wells. Conservation keeps the underground bank balanced.

items.prompt: Legendary: picture ALL of Earth's water as exactly 1,000 bottles, with 970 of them salty ocean water. Of the freshwater bottles that remain, two-thirds are frozen in glaciers and ice sheets — so how many bottles of UNFROZEN freshwater are left?
items.hint: Count the freshwater bottles first, then remove the frozen two-thirds.
items.explanation: 1,000 − 970 = 30 fresh bottles; two-thirds of those (20) are ice, leaving just 10. And most of THOSE hide underground — the whole world runs on a tiny liquid sliver.

items.prompt: Why does the Moon change shape every night? (Spoiler: it doesn't.)

steps.text: The Moon makes no light of its own — it's a giant rock mirror reflecting sunlight. At every moment, the half facing the Sun is lit and the other half is dark.
As the Moon orbits Earth (a full lap of phases takes about 29.5 days), we view its lit half from changing angles — sometimes the whole lit face, sometimes a sliver, sometimes none.

check.question: So a 'phase' is really…
options: How much of the Moon's lit half WE can see from Earth
How much of the Moon Earth's shadow covers
How much of the Moon is actually glowing

steps.text: New moon: the Moon sits roughly between Earth and the Sun, so its lit side faces away from us. Full moon: the Moon is on the far side of Earth from the Sun, so we see the entire lit face.

Earth's shadow is NOT the cause — it only touches the Moon during a rare lunar eclipse. Whoa bonus: the same side of the Moon always faces Earth, so no human saw the far side until a spacecraft flew around it in 1959.

check.question: When DOES Earth's shadow touch the Moon?
options: Every single night
Only during a lunar eclipse
Whenever the Moon is full

items.prompt: Why is June warm in New Jersey but chilly in Australia? Complete the expedition log.

lines: Earth's axis is tilted about [[23.5|23]] degrees, and the tilt points the same way all year.
In June the NORTHERN half leans toward the Sun — sunlight strikes it more directly and days last longer, so it's [[summer]] there.
Meanwhile the southern half leans away, so Australians are wearing [[winter]] coats in June.

items.hint: The tilt decides which half gets the direct, high-noon-style sunlight — and that half gets the warm season.
items.explanation: Seasons come from the 23.5° tilt, which controls how directly sunlight lands and how long days last. Fun twist: Earth is actually CLOSEST to the Sun in January!

items.prompt: The Moon shines bright on a clear night. Where does that light actually come from?
items.answer: It's reflected sunlight — the Moon makes no light of its own
options: It's reflected sunlight — the Moon makes no light of its own
The Moon glows from hot lava under its surface
The Moon burns like a small star
City lights from Earth bounce off it
items.hint: The Moon is basically a giant gray mirror.
items.explanation: Moonlight is recycled sunlight bouncing off gray rock. Whoa fact: that rock is about as dark as an asphalt road — it only looks brilliant against the black sky.

items.prompt: Amal's baking bench holds solid butter, liquid milk, and oven steam. Sort each particle report into the right state of matter.

Solid: particles locked in a tidy pattern, vibrating in place
keeps its own shape no matter the container
Liquid: particles touching but sliding past each other
takes the container's shape but keeps the same volume
Gas: particles far apart, zooming in every direction
spreads out to fill the entire container

items.hint: Ask two questions: do the particles hold a fixed shape, and do they stay together at all?
items.explanation: States of matter are all about particle grip: locked in place, sliding past, or flying free. Heating just turns up the particle dance music!

items.prompt: Earth's rocky outer shell is cracked into more than a dozen giant slabs that creep along a few centimeters per year. What are these slabs called?
options: Tectonic plates
Continents
Lava shelves
Core fragments
items.hint: The continents RIDE on these — they aren't the slabs themselves.
items.explanation: Tectonic plates carry both continents AND ocean floor on their backs. They drift about as fast as your fingernails grow.

items.prompt: Complete the field note from the Tiny Worlds expedition.

lines: Amal, her cat, and a sunflower are all built from trillions of tiny [[cells]] — the basic building blocks of every living thing.

items.hint: Same word as a honeycomb's little rooms — that's where the name came from.
items.explanation: Robert Hooke coined 'cells' in 1665 because cork under his microscope looked like tiny rooms. Whoa fact: your body holds roughly 37 trillion of them.

items.prompt: An ice cube's diary, from freezer to steam. Fill in the particle story.

lines: Ice: my particles sit locked in a tidy pattern, only vibrating in place — I'm a [[solid]].
Melted in the warm kitchen: my particles still touch but slide past each other — now I'm a [[liquid]].
Boiled away: my particles zoom far apart and spread through the whole room — I've become a [[gas|vapor|vapour]].

items.hint: Track the particle grip: locked, sliding, flying free.
items.explanation: Same particles, three costumes — heat just speeds them up until they break formation. That's all melting and boiling really are!

items.prompt: Amal logs the Moon every night, Duolingo-streak style. Put the first half of the cycle in order.
items.hint: Start invisible, then grow the lit sliver night by night.
items.explanation: The lit part waxes (grows) from new to full over about two weeks. Whoa fact: in Swahili, 'mwezi' means both moon AND month — the Moon's cycle is where months come from!

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about the Moon — tap the lie.

truths: At every moment, half of the Moon is lit by the Sun
The same side of the Moon always faces Earth
data.lie: The Moon's phases are caused by Earth's shadow falling on it

items.hint: Earth's shadow only reaches the Moon on special, rare nights.
items.explanation: Phases happen because we see different amounts of the Moon's sunlit half as it orbits us. Earth's shadow touches the Moon only during a lunar eclipse — a few times a year at most.

items.prompt: Herbology homework at wizard school: label the parts of this plant cell.
items.hint: Two bank words don't belong on this diagram: one is a green chemical, not a structure, and one isn't pictured.
items.explanation: Nucleus = control center, chloroplasts = sunlight kitchens, the wall = armor, the vacuole = water tank. Chlorophyll is the green pigment INSIDE chloroplasts, not a separate part.

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about why seasons happen — find the lie.

truths: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees as it orbits the Sun
When New Jersey has summer, Australia has winter
data.lie: Summer comes when Earth swings closest to the Sun

items.hint: Surprise: look up WHEN Earth is actually closest to the Sun.
items.explanation: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January — the middle of northern WINTER! Seasons come from the tilt, which controls how directly sunlight strikes and how long days last.

items.prompt: Match each cell part to its job.

pairs: Nucleus
the control center holding the cell's instructions (DNA)
Chloroplast
captures sunlight and makes food for the plant
Cell wall
the stiff outer layer that gives a plant cell its support
Vacuole
the storage tank that holds water and keeps the cell plump
Mitochondrion
the power station that releases energy from food

items.hint: Think castle: a command room, a kitchen, walls, a cistern, and a furnace.
items.explanation: Every part is a tiny machine with a job. Mitochondria are powering YOUR cells right now — billions of microscopic furnaces burning your breakfast.

items.prompt: It's July in New Jersey, and the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun. What actually makes the days hotter?
items.answer: Sunlight strikes more directly AND daylight lasts longer
options: Sunlight strikes more directly AND daylight lasts longer
Earth is at its closest point to the Sun in July
The Sun itself burns hotter during the summer months
The Moon reflects extra heat onto Earth in summer
items.hint: Think of a flashlight: shining straight down versus at a slant.
items.explanation: The tilt aims the hemisphere so rays land head-on (concentrated) and the Sun stays up longer. Distance is innocent — Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January.

items.prompt: During a NEW moon we see no moon at all. Where is the Moon during this phase?
items.answer: Roughly between Earth and the Sun, with its lit side facing away from us
options: Roughly between Earth and the Sun, with its lit side facing away from us
On the opposite side of Earth from the Sun
Hidden inside Earth's shadow
Below Earth, near the South Pole
items.hint: The lit half always faces the Sun — where must the Moon be for us to face only the dark half?
items.explanation: At new moon the Moon sits sunward of us, showing Earth its unlit back. Whoa fact: that means the new moon is up in the DAYTIME sky, rising and setting with the Sun.

items.prompt: Amal compares cells from her cat and from the catnip plant under a microscope. Sort each part.
items.hint: The plant-only parts are all about standing tall and cooking with sunlight.
items.explanation: Cat cells skip the wall and chloroplasts — animals eat food instead of making it, and skeletons handle the support. Both kinds still need a nucleus, a membrane, and mitochondria.

items.prompt: A mole-geologist's report on drifting continents contains one error. Tap it.

segments: Earth's outer shell is broken into tectonic plates that ride on hot, soft rock below.
The plates creep along at about the speed your fingernails grow.
Most earthquakes and volcanoes happen near the quiet CENTERS of plates.
Around 250 million years ago, the continents were joined in one supercontinent called Pangaea.

items.hint: Where do two plates grind, crash, and dive past each other — in the middle, or at the edges?
items.explanation: The action is at the EDGES: plates collide, slide, and split at their boundaries, which is where most quakes and volcanoes strike. Plate centers are comparatively calm.

items.prompt: Legendary: the Atlantic Ocean grows about 2.5 centimeters wider every year. At that rate, how many KILOMETERS wider will it be in one million years? (100 cm = 1 m, 1000 m = 1 km)
items.hint: Multiply first, then climb the unit ladder: cm to m to km.
items.explanation: 2.5 cm × 1,000,000 = 2,500,000 cm = 25,000 m = 25 km. That's how Pangaea fell apart — fingernail speed, given a few hundred million years.

items.prompt: Legendary: tonight is a FULL moon, and Amal's favorite K-pop group drops their album at the next NEW moon. About how long is the wait?
items.answer: About 2 weeks — new moon is halfway through the 29.5-day cycle
options: About 2 weeks — new moon is halfway through the 29.5-day cycle
About a month — phases repeat every 29.5 days
About 2 days — phases change quickly
About 6 months — the Moon moves slowly
items.hint: Full and new sit at OPPOSITE points of the cycle — what fraction of the lap is that?
items.explanation: Full to new is half the 29.5-day cycle, so roughly 15 days. A full month is only the wait from new moon back to new moon.
